papers.title: Evaluating Bayesian deep learning for robust biomedical time-series classification under distribution shift: A sleep scoring case study
papers.abstract: In biomedical time-series classification, machine learning models often suffer from deteriorating accuracy and calibration due to distribution shift. We investigate to what degree Bayesian-inspired deep learning improves robustness through Bayesian model averaging (BMA). Using rodent sleep scoring as a case study, we evaluate BMA under distribution shifts in genotype, laboratory, and species. We systematically compare nine approximate inference methods spanning single- and multi-basin approaches across two neural network backbones on in-distribution (ID) data and five out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets. In our results, multi-basin methods perform best, outperforming baselines and single-basin methods. Compared with point estimates, BMA generally improves OOD accuracy and calibration across both architectures, while yielding only modest ID gains. It also often improves selective prediction and OOD and artifact detection, but, interestingly, not inter-rater disagreement detection.

papers.title: Behavioral evidence for two-stage sleep in spiders.
papers.abstract: Sleep is a fundamental behavioral state found across the animal kingdom, yet most of what we know about sleep is heavily vertebrate-biased. Studies are scarce or nonexistent in all but a few invertebrate lineages. A recent study of an REM sleep-like behavior in a jumping spider has reported unexpected parallels to sleep expression in vertebrates. So far, experimental evidence that these behavioral indicators truly represent sleep was lacking in spiders. Here, we present a comprehensive investigation into sleep behavior in the spider Portia fimbriata (Salticidae). We demonstrate diurnal activity, a free-running circadian rhythm, robust sleep architecture, regularly occurring REM-like behaviors, elevated arousal thresholds during those REM-like states, as well as rebound effects following sleep disruption. We conclude that the behavior we observe in spiders is behavioral sleep, providing evidence for an REM-like sleep substate in a terrestrial invertebrate. These results contribute to fundamental questions about the evolution and function of sleep across animals.

papers.title: Closed-Loop Acoustic Stimulation of Slow Oscillations Using a Wireless EEG Headband: A Polysomnography-Validated Feasibility Study.
papers.abstract: Acoustic stimulation precisely timed during sleep can enhance slow oscillations (SOs), a hallmark of deep sleep that is critical for restorative sleep. To date, this approach has largely been restricted to laboratory settings using high-density electroencephalography (EEG). Wearable EEG systems featuring closed-loop acoustic stimulation could enable scalable, home-based approaches to modulating slow-wave sleep. Here, we tested whether a real-time modeling approach (M-CLNS) could be implemented using a wireless EEG headband with forehead electrodes in healthy participants. Acoustic stimulation was delivered during a single night of sleep in alternating stimulation and sham conditions. We evaluated the accuracy of SO phase targeting utilizing the EEG headband and assessed whether it could be used to detect stimulation-induced changes in oscillatory dynamics. The findings were validated against simultaneous polysomnographic (PSG) recordings as an independent reference. We found that SO phase was targeted consistently near the intended phase using the headband, despite reduced amplitude and signal quality compared with simultaneous PSG. Acoustic stimulation produced an immediate enhancement of SO dynamics, as well as sustained increases in SO density and power spectral density within the SO and delta frequency range (0.75-5 Hz) during deep sleep. These effects were apparent both in the EEG headband and PSG signals. These results demonstrate the feasibility of closed-loop acoustic stimulation using a wireless EEG headband, providing a foundation for future home-based and clinical applications.

papers.title: Sleep Variables in Health Research: From Systematic Omission to Methodological Integration - A Narrative Review and Proposal.
papers.abstract: For decades, sample characterization in health and physiological research has relied on a "triad of convenience": demographics, anthropometrics, and socioeconomic status. While these parameters offer a baseline description, they systematically omit a critical biological variable sustaining human homeostasis: sleep. This baseline omission introduces significant residual confounding, creating a "Table 1 Fallacy" where matched cohorts appear identical but remain physiologically heterogeneous due to unmeasured sleep-wake variance, including duration, quality, and circadian alignment. Sleep occupies a unique position among neglected baseline variables because it simultaneously coordinates neuroendocrine secretion, immune priming, autonomic regulation, and metabolic clearance within each circadian cycle, mechanistic roles that differentiate it from other lifestyle factors currently absent from reporting guidelines. Compelling evidence demonstrates that sleep duration, quality, and chronotype directly modulate peripheral insulin sensitivity, hormonal balance, immune readiness, and cardiovascular function. Failing to account for these metrics can lead to the misclassification of participants as "non-responders" in clinical trials, masking true primary intervention effects or creating an illusion of treatment efficacy. To restore reproducibility and scientific rigor, we contend that sleep reporting must transition from a voluntary act to a methodological mandate in studies where sleep represents a biologically plausible source of confounding. We propose a high-yield, low-cost Minimal Sleep Set (MSS) utilizing validated screening tools to systematically control for sleep-wake variance, ensuring that the human biological state is as clearly defined as the intervention itself.

papers.title: High-fat diet-induced MAFLD is associated with sleep architecture disruption via hippocampal neuroinflammation and bifurcated IRS-1/Akt/mTOR signaling in mice.
papers.abstract: Epidemiological associations between metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) and sleep disturbances point to shared mechanisms, yet the underlying central pathways remain unexplored. We hypothesized that high-fat diet (HFD)-induced MAFLD disrupts sleep architecture via hippocampal neuroinflammation and dysregulation of the IRS-1/Akt/mTOR signaling axis. Male BALB/c mice were fed a control diet (CD) or a 60% HFD for 16 weeks to induce MAFLD. Sleep-wake architecture was assessed by 24-h EEG/EMG recordings. We evaluated hepatic steatosis, serum cytokines, hippocampal histology, and hippocampal pro-inflammatory cytokines. Hippocampal expression and phosphorylation of IRS-1 (Ser307), Akt (Ser473), and mTOR (Ser2448) were analyzed by Western blot. HFD-fed mice developed hepatic steatosis, elevated liver enzymes, and increased serum tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β). These mice exhibited reduced non‑rapid eye movement (NREM) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep duration, severe sleep fragmentation (reflected by increased bout numbers and shorter mean bout durations), and diminished NREM sleep delta power. Cosinor analysis revealed a dampened circadian rhythm of NREM sleep delta power. In the hippocampus, HFD induced neuronal injury, elevated TNF-α and IL-1β levels, accompanied by a bifurcated signaling profile: increased p-IRS-1 (Ser307), decreased p-Akt (Ser473), and elevated p-mTOR (Ser2448). Our findings identify a putative liver-hippocampus-sleep axis in which MAFLD-driven systemic inflammation and hippocampal IRS-1/Akt/mTOR dysregulation are associated with profound sleep disruption, providing a framework for future mechanistic validation. Targeting this axis may offer new therapeutic strategies for sleep disorders in MAFLD.

papers.title: Accurate EEG-based linear state-space model of cortical dynamics during a passive motor task with exogenous input.
papers.abstract: Revealing the dynamics of the brain in the presence of exogenous inputs iscrucial for mechanistic understanding, interventions and regulations. We study state-spacemathematical modeling of brain's cortical dynamics using electroencephalography (EEG)data in an experiment with continuous exogenous input. We use subspaceidentification techniques to model the brain dynamics in a passive motor task experiment.The EEG data were recorded while participants were seated with their wrist strapped to ahaptic manipulator. The manipulator imposed a continuous multisine angularperturbation to the wrist as the exogenous input to the brain. Using twosubspace identification algorithms, we show that linear time-invariant state-space modelsaccurately represent the measurements, in a latent space, assuming that the EEG data arethe models' output. The model is verified and validated using data from sevenparticipants. Moreover, we construct linear maps to relate the latent space dynamics tothe neural source space. We verify that the findings of our model align with thoseidentified in previous studies. Accurate linear model in the presence ofexogenous input provides a pathway for designing parsimonious and simple controllers. Inaddition, it enables development of online monitoring, connectivity analysis and controlrelevant to neurorehabilitation, motor learning, and brain-computer interfacing.

papers.title: Automated Sleep Staging Performance Across Two Experimental Sleep Manipulation Protocols in Adolescents.
papers.abstract: Automated sleep staging algorithms improve the scalability of polysomnography analysis in adolescent research but are primarily validated in undisturbed, single-night sleep recordings. It remains unclear whether these algorithms maintain performance when sleep architecture is experimentally manipulated. This study evaluated the validity of two popular automated sleep staging approaches across two distinct sleep manipulation paradigms in adolescents: a sleep restriction protocol (N=43, mean age [SD]=13.37[1.06] years; four nights including two sleep extension [10hr] and two restriction [4hr] nights) and a slow-wave sleep deprivation (SWSD) protocol (N=18, mean age [SD]=17.17[1.79] years; baseline, SWSD, and recovery nights). Automated sleep staging was performed using the POPulation-level Sleep Stager (POPS), the Yet Another Spindle Algorithm (YASA), and combined POPS+YASA. Manual polysomnography scoring by experienced sleep technicians served as the reference standard. Agreement was assessed using Cohen's k, and stage-specific performance was evaluated using F1 scores and confusion matrices. Mixed-effects models tested differences in overall and stage-specific agreement across nights. All staging approaches demonstrated moderate-to-substantial agreement with manual scoring across manipulated sleep conditions (k range; range=0.53-0.76). In the sleep restriction study, agreement was lower in restricted versus extended sleep (P<0.05), and agreement declined across restriction nights, with poorer Wake, N1, and N2 classification, while N3 remained preserved. In the SWSD study, overall agreement was lower on the SWSD night, with poorer N3 classification while other stages were preserved. Automated sleep staging performance may be less consistent in adolescents when sleep is curtailed or fragmented; future studies should develop and validate these algorithms under multiple sleep conditions.

papers.title: Sleep and Drowsiness in Cattle: A Narrative Review of Physiology, Measurement, and Methodological Challenges.
papers.abstract: Sleep in cattle is a complex physiological state comprising non-rapid eye movement (NREM) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, while drowsing represents an intermediate vigilance state between wakefulness and sleep. Research has progressed from invasive electrophysiological recordings to noninvasive polysomnography (PSG), behavioral assessment, accelerometry, and automated classification approaches. However, accurately identifying and quantifying vigilance states under production conditions remains challenging. This narrative review, based on 22 primary studies identified through searches of Web of Science, Scopus and Google Scholar, critically synthesizes current knowledge of sleep physiology in cattle, the approaches used to assess it, and the principal methodological limitations affecting interpretation of the available evidence. Cattle exhibit a polyphasic sleep pattern, with NREM generally accounting for the largest proportion of total sleep. However, reported sleep and drowsing durations vary considerably among studies, and these differences may reflect both biological variation and methodological factors. Drowsing is particularly difficult to characterize because its behavioral and physiological features overlap with quiet wakefulness and light sleep. Rumination represents an additional challenge because associated muscular activity can interfere with electrophysiological recordings and complicate vigilance-state classification. Behavioral observations and accelerometry provide scalable measures of resting and sleep-like behavior but cannot independently establish physiological sleep, whereas PSG provides greater physiological resolution while remaining susceptible to artifacts and practical constraints. Current evidence is insufficient to establish causal relationships between sleep variation and cattle health, welfare, or productive performance. Future research should improve physiological classification during overlapping behavioral states, better validate scalable monitoring approaches, and evaluate the functional consequences of sleep variation across diverse cattle populations and production conditions.

papers.title: A Unified Flexible Large Polysomnography Model for Sleep Staging and Downstream Clinical Screening
papers.abstract: Polysomnography (PSG) is central to sleep medicine, yet its analysis remains hindered by labor-intensive manual scoring and limited cross-center generalizability. We present LPSGM, a large-scale PSG model trained on 220,500 hours of data from 16 public datasets (24,000 recordings) that addresses two challenges: cross-center sleep staging generalization and PSG-based screening of narcolepsy, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), and depression. LPSGM integrates domain-adaptive pre-training, flexible channel configurations, and a unified architecture to accommodate heterogeneous recording protocols. In prospective validation, LPSGM achieves expert-level sleep staging ({kappa} = 0.845 {+/-} 0.066 vs. inter-expert {kappa} = 0.850 {+/-} 0.102) and matches fully supervised models on independent private cohorts. For downstream screening, LPSGM achieves 84.2% accuracy ({kappa} = 0.761) in three-class narcolepsy classification, with cross-institutional transfer for normal-versus-abnormal hypersomnia yielding an AUC of 0.879. Severe OSA screening reaches an AUC of 0.874 without access to respiratory signals. Depression symptom screening achieves an AUC of 0.801 in a surrogate-labeled APPLES cohort, and cross-dataset transfer to an independent clinically diagnosed cohort reaches an AUC of 0.965. These results suggest that LPSGM's pre-trained representations capture sleep-related signatures that generalize across institutions and support PSG-based screening of clinically relevant conditions. The code and pre-trained model are publicly available at https://github.com/Deng-GuiFeng/LPSGM.

papers.title: Characterising sleep spindle emergence in infancy: Effects of prematurity and early locomotor intervention
papers.abstract: Study objectives: Sleep spindles are thalamocortical oscillations evolving during early brain maturation. In adults, they support memory consolidation and are organised into rhythmic "trains" thought to support memory reactivation. How this temporal organisation emerges in infancy, and whether prematurity or early sensorimotor experience shapes it, remains unclear. This study characterised infant spindles and investigated how prematurity and early locomotor training affect their temporal and spatial organisation, providing insight into early brain maturation. Methods: Daytime high-density EEG sleep recordings were analysed in 50 infants born full-term (n=12) or very preterm (n=38, including 12 who received locomotor training) at 2 months corrected age. Spindle temporal organisation was analysed using a two-step Morlet wavelet transform to quantify slow modulations of spindle-band power (11-16Hz). Time-frequency decomposition around spindle onset was used to identify significant spindle-band scalp-wide activity, and topographical maps were statistically compared between groups. Results: All groups showed rhythmic spindle organisation, three times slower than in adults, with no group differences. Untrained preterm infants showed a more diffuse spindle-band activity than the distinct frontal and central clusters observed in full-term infants. Trained preterm infants exhibited a spatial distribution closely resembling that of full-term infants, although their frontal spindle density was lower than in both other groups. Conclusions: Spindle rhythmic organisation emerged early in infancy and remained unaffected by prematurity or locomotor training. Prematurity was associated with more diffuse spindle-band activity, suggesting reduced cortical specialisation, whereas trained preterm infants showed a spatial distribution resembling that of full-term infants, suggesting that early locomotor experience may influence thalamocortical organisation.

papers.title: RefineSleepNet: Task-Driven Signal-Domain Transformation for EEG/EOG Sleep Staging.
papers.abstract: Automatic sleep staging relies on effective representation of physiological signals. Representative raw-signal sleep-staging encoders typically transform input waveforms while progressively compressing their temporal resolution within the same encoding path. However, explicit modality-specific, sample-aligned, and task-driven signal-domain transformation before epoch-level feature extraction remains comparatively underexplored. To investigate this design, we propose RefineSleepNet, an end-to-end sequence-to-sequence framework that explicitly separates these two stages. Separately parameterized Signal Refinement U-Net (SRU-Net) branches first transform EEG and EOG waveforms while preserving the original temporal length, after which Epoch Feature Extractors (EFEs) extract epoch-level representations from the refined signals. Fused Sequence Attention (FSA) then performs multimodal integration and cross-epoch contextual modeling before epoch-wise classification. All stages are jointly optimized using the final sleep-staging objective without a separate waveform reconstruction target. RefineSleepNet was evaluated on Sleep-EDF-39, Sleep-EDF-153, and ISRUC-3 using subject-independent 10-fold cross-validation, achieving accuracy/macro-F1 (MF1) scores of 84.5%/79.8%, 83.5%/78.1%, and 80.3%/78.1%, respectively. Ablation experiments supported the coordinated design, while statistical analysis and intermediate-representation evaluations further examined the robustness and characteristics of the learned transformation. The learned transformation retained broad temporal and spectral organization while introducing local waveform changes and modality-specific spectral redistribution. These results support the staged organization as a viable modeling strategy for EEG/EOG sleep staging.

papers.title: CSPT-SleepNet: An Automatic Sleep Staging Framework Integrating Center-Driven Sequence Supervision and Multimodal Pyramid Token Encoding.
papers.abstract: Background: Automatic sleep staging is fundamental to sleep architecture analysis and the diagnosis of sleep disorders. Sleep staging requires jointly modeling complementary information across modalities, multi-scale physiological features, and temporal relationships across consecutive epochs. In target epoch prediction from consecutive epochs, non-target epochs primarily provide contextual information, but their ground-truth labels remain underused as auxiliary supervision. Methods: We propose CSPT-SleepNet, an automatic sleep staging framework integrating center-driven sequence supervision with multimodal pyramid token encoding. A Multimodal Pyramid Token Encoder extracts hierarchical multi-scale features from electroencephalogram, electrooculogram, and electromyogram signals, followed by intra-modal, cross-modal, and inter-epoch modeling for center-epoch classification. During training, the center epoch receives primary classification supervision, while non-center epochs receive weaker auxiliary supervision based on their ground-truth labels, providing stage-informed contextual support for the prediction target. Results: In subject-independent cross-validation on Sleep-EDF-20, Sleep-EDF-78, and ISRUC-S3, CSPT-SleepNet achieved accuracy (ACC)/macro F1 (MF1) scores of 87.93%/83.53%, 85.81%/80.87%, and 84.06%/82.86%, respectively. In a separate controlled comparison on Sleep-EDF-20, center-driven sequence supervision improved ACC and MF1 by 0.60 and 0.91 percentage points, respectively, over equal-weight sequence supervision. The full model has 3.418 million trainable parameters and requires 397.10 million floating-point operations for an input sequence of nine 30-s epochs. Conclusions: CSPT-SleepNet provides an effective framework for center-epoch sleep staging from consecutive multimodal inputs. Nevertheless, N1 recognition remains challenging, with F1 scores ranging from 55.3% to 62.7% across the three datasets.

papers.title: Ketones and Sleep: A Narrative Review of Mechanisms, Preclinical Models, and Human Evidence.
papers.abstract: Sleep is a metabolically dynamic state, and ketone bodies may interact with sleep physiology as both oxidative substrates and signaling metabolites. β-Hydroxybutyrate (BHB), acetoacetate (AcAc), and acetone rise during fasting, carbohydrate restriction, ketogenic diets used for therapeutic or non-therapeutic purposes, prolonged exercise, selected pathological states of insulin deficiency, and after consumption of exogenous ketones. This narrative review synthesizes mechanistic, preclinical, and human evidence linking endogenously generated ketosis and ketosis generated from exogenous ketone consumption to sleep architecture, sleep quality, sleep-disordered breathing, and sleep-relevant metabolic pathways. We reviewed studies involving ketogenic diets, fasting or caloric restriction, and consumption of exogenous ketones, prioritizing investigations with polysomnography, electroencephalography (EEG), sleep architecture, respiratory, or validated sleep-questionnaire outcomes, while also considering mechanistic studies of neuronal excitability, inflammation, epigenetic regulation, circadian timing, and brain energetics. The most direct preclinical evidence indicates that AcAc, but not BHB, increases slow-wave activity (delta power 0.5-4 Hz) during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and suppresses glutamate release in mice, supporting a potential role for ketone metabolism in sleep homeostasis. Dietary, fasting, and aging models further suggest that lipid/ketone metabolism can alter NREM/rapid eye movement (REM) balance, circadian metabolic rhythms, and sleep-wake responses to energetic stress, with aged-rat data showing sex-specific REM and cognitive effects of ketogenic interventions. Human studies are suggestive but heterogeneous: acute carbohydrate restriction can increase slow-wave sleep and reduce REM sleep in healthy adults; ketogenic therapies may improve subjective sleep in selected neurological and metabolic populations; and ketone ester ingestion can improve sleep efficiency after strenuous evening exercise, but not during hypoxia-induced sleep disruption. Ketones are sleep-relevant metabolic signals, but their effects are conditional rather than universally sleep-promoting. They may also indirectly affect sleep by enhancing wakefulness quality. The ketone concentration range associated with optimal sleep outcomes remains undefined, and potential dose-, timing-, and context-dependent effects on sleep require further study. Future studies should distinguish AcAc from BHB biology, measure nocturnal ketone dynamics, incorporate PSG/EEG spectral endpoints, and separate ketosis-specific effects from weight loss, energy deficit, exercise load, respiratory physiology, circadian timing, and disease-related confounders.

papers.title: Circadian patterns of device-detected postoperative atrial fibrillation during 2.5 years of continuous monitoring after cardiac surgery: The RACE V-Tissue Bank Study.
papers.abstract: Postoperative atrial fibrillation (POAF) is common after cardiac surgery. AF in non-surgical patients exhibits distinct circadian patterns (adrenergic/daytime and vagal/nocturnal), but such patterns for new-onset POAF and recurrent AF remain undefined. This study aimed to characterize circadian AF patterns and relate chronotypes to clinical, biochemical, histological, and outcome features. Patients undergoing first cardiac surgery, with and without preoperative AF, were continuously monitored for 2.5 years with an implantable loop recorder. Early AF was defined as AF within 30 days. Patients with sustained AF (≥20 episodes) were chronotyped via circular statistics and local regression of episode duration and ventricular rate (Vrate), and classified as adrenergic, vagal, mixed, or non-rhythmic. Preoperative imaging, electrocardiography, biomarkers, and paired atrial histology were compared across chronotypes. Of the 98 patients (71 without and 27 with preoperative AF), 53 (54.1%) developed POAF (3607 episodes). Patients with prior AF showed a morning onset peak, whereas new-onset POAF showed a uniform 24-hour distribution. Of 26 patients with sustained AF, 20 were rhythmic (9 adrenergic, 7 vagal, 4 mixed), and 6 were non-rhythmic; 27 had incidental AF (<20 episodes). Rhythmic AF correlated with larger atrial volumes, prolonged PR intervals, higher bone morphogenetic protein-10 levels, and greater right-atrial endomysial fibrosis and asymmetry, most pronounced in the mixed chronotype. Adrenergic AF was associated with more arrhythmia-related emergency visits and cardioversions. AF after cardiac surgery comprises distinct circadian subtypes. New-onset POAF and recurrent AF display different circadian patterns, and individual chronotypes are associated with varying degrees of atrial remodeling and clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Epithelial function of the circadian clock gene, Bmal1, in regulating the mucosa.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms, 24-hour repeating oscillations in daily physiology, are implicated in maintaining intestinal homeostasis. These rhythms are driven by the circadian clock, a molecular timekeeper found throughout cells of the body, including those of the intestinal epithelium. Loss of clock function has been found to worsen colitis; however, it is not clear how the clock impacts regeneration which enables a tissue to return to its homeostatic set point following an injury. To investigate these questions, we used a conditional knockout of the core clock gene, Bmal1, in mouse colon epithelial cells. Our data show that prior to injury Bmal1 promotes colon mucus production, which increases in thickness and abundance within goblet cells when mice are active and begin feeding. Bmal1 loss lowers mucus production but does not drive an apparent tissue phenotype until the system is injured and regenerates itself. In this context, Bmal1 epithelial loss drives a male-specific colitis exacerbation and a delay in the ability of colon epithelial cells of both male and female mice to resolve injury to return to their homeostatic set point. Our data suggest that epithelial sex-specific clock rhythms are needed for optimal colon barrier homeostasis.

papers.title: Effects of Circadian Phase and Exercise Training on Systemic and Tissue-Specific Redox Responses in Mice Fed a High-Fat Diet.
papers.abstract: The effects of exercise timing on redox adaptation under high-fat diet (HFD)-induced metabolic stress remain unclear. We investigated whether the circadian phase of training alters systemic and tissue-specific redox responses in HFD-fed mice. Male C57BL/6J mice fed an HFD remained sedentary or underwent 8 weeks of treadmill training at Zeitgeber time 3 (ZT3) or Zeitgeber time 15 (ZT15). Samples were collected 48 h after the final session. Plasma redox status was assessed using the OXY-adsorbent test (OXY), the derivatives of reactive oxygen metabolites test (d-ROMs; mainly reflecting circulating hydroperoxides), and the biological antioxidant potential test (BAP), and redox and inflammatory gene expression levels were quantified in three skeletal muscles and the liver. Exercise increased BAP (p = 0.0442), whereas OXY was unchanged. The phase × exercise interaction for d-ROMs showed a nonsignificant trend (p = 0.0560); exploratory comparisons showed higher d-ROMs in ZT15-sedentary (sed) than in ZT3-sed and ZT15-exercise (exe) mice. papers.title: Indirect Skin Homeostasis Modulation by an Essential Oil Blend in Mice with Insomnia Comorbid Anxiety: Sensitivity of Dermal Fibroblasts to Exogenously Applied Circulating Molecules.

Although the concept of "emotional skincare" has attracted growing research interest, experimental evidence supporting the indirect skin-protective effects of essential oils through emotional regulation remains limited. This study investigates the indirect effect of an essential oil blend (EOB) on skin homeostasis in mice with insomnia comorbid anxiety (ICA, a pharmacologically validated emotional stress model induced by para-chlorophenylalanine) and aims to profile the sensitivity of dermal fibroblasts to candidate circulating molecules identified from EOB-treated ICA mice, thereby laying a mechanistic foundation for emotional skincare research. Methods: An essential oil blend (EOB) comprising lavender, Kushui rose, sweet orange, Roman chamomile, sandalwood, and clary sage essential oils was prepared. An ICA mouse model was established using para-chlorophenylalanine. Behavioral phenotypes, as well as neurotransmitter and hormonal indices, were measured to validate the anxiolytic and sleep disturbance-alleviating effects of EOB administered via intraperitoneal injection at 300 mg/kg per injection (two injections overall). Skin histological alterations and circulating biomarker profiles were evaluated, and selected differentially altered circulating molecules were exogenously applied to cultured dermal fibroblasts in vitro to assess their effects on fibroblast functions. Results: EOB significantly alleviated ICA-like behaviors and ameliorated abnormal levels of brain neurotransmitters and hormones in mice. Although only mild histological variations were observed in the skin after EOB intervention, significant alterations in cortisol, melatonin, 5-hydroxytryptamine, interleukin-10, and type I collagen were detected in serum or skin tissues. Exogenous application of these circulating molecules elicited differential responses in dermal fibroblasts, affecting oxidative stress, inflammatory responses, and extracellular matrix synthesis in a molecule-specific manner. Notably, these fibroblast assays only demonstrate cellular sensitivity in vitro and do not prove that these circulating molecules directly mediate the in vivo effects observed in mice. Conclusions: EOB intervention ameliorates insomnia- and anxiety-related behaviors and concurrent favorable changes in skin-associated molecular profiles in ICA mice. These changes are accompanied by alterations in circulating bioactive molecules to which dermal fibroblasts exhibit measurable sensitivity in vitro. These observations are consistent with, but do not definitively establish, a brain-skin axis-mediated mechanism. These findings provide preliminary experimental evidence for the emotional skincare concept and identify candidate circulating molecules for future causal validation; the in vivo regulatory roles of these molecules and the precise signaling pathways involved remain to be established in dedicated mechanistic studies.

papers.title: Sex differences in sleep and memory relationships in older adults at risk for Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: Biological sex is an important modifier of aging and Alzheimer's disease risk, yet the sleep-related mechanisms through which sex and genetic risk interact to influence memory remain poorly understood. We examined whether associations among non-rapid eye movement sleep physiology, overnight memory retention, and apolipoprotein E ϵ4 (APOE ϵ4) status, a genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease, differed by sex in cognitively unimpaired older adults enriched for Alzheimer's disease risk. Eighty participants completed overnight polysomnography with high-density electroencephalography, and 65 also completed an evening encoding/immediate recall and morning delayed recall word-pair memory task. Overnight memory retention did not differ by sex. However, exploratory analyses of the proportional overnight retention measure suggested a sex × APOE ϵ4 interaction, such that female APOE ϵ4 carriers may exhibit reduced overnight forgetting relative to female non-carriers and male carriers. Although counterintuitive, this pattern may reflect compensatory or resilience-related sleep-memory mechanisms in cognitively unimpaired women at genetic risk for Alzheimer's disease rather than a protective effect of APOE ϵ4 itself. Women spent more time in N3 sleep and had higher non-rapid eye movement delta and slow sigma power than men. Sleep-memory associations also differed by sex: greater N2 duration was more strongly associated with better overnight retention in men, whereas greater frontal slow sigma power and fronto-central fast sigma power were positively associated with retention in women. Exploratory APOE-stratified analyses suggested sex-specific differences in sleep stage-memory relationships, with more positive N2-memory associations in male than female APOE ϵ4 carriers and more positive N3-memory associations in female than male carriers; both differences remained significant after FDR correction. TFCE-corrected analyses further identified positive associations between NREM delta and sigma activity and overnight memory retention in female APOE ϵ4 carriers. These findings highlight sex-specific patterns in NREM sleep physiology and sleep-memory relationships in cognitively unimpaired older adults at risk for Alzheimer's disease. More broadly, the results suggest that sex and APOE ϵ4 status may jointly shape the neurophysiological pathways linking sleep and memory, underscoring the importance of considering sex as a biological variable when studying sleep, cognitive aging, and Alzheimer's disease vulnerability.

Increasing Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, ALS, Huntington's, frontotemporal dementia, Lewy body disease, PTSD, and vascular cognitive impairment due to impaired glymphatic axonal clearance/blood-brain barrier dysregulation/synaptic degeneration/pathoproteopathic protein We examine how clock genes, melatonin signaling, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis administration, microglia reactivity, and immune-mediated metabolic dysregulation affect dementia. New endocrine, transcriptomic, multi-omics, and wearable-derived digital biomarkers, chronopharmacology (including melatonin receptor agonists), bright-light therapy, time-restricted eating with exercise chronotherapy guidance/synchronization, sleep optimization, and gut microbiota modulation This study addressed inter-individual circadian variability, genetic susceptibility to therapy timing, biomarker standardization, and clinical trial design. The melatonin-cortisol axis may identify and treat age-related neurodegenerative diseases with tailored treatment.

Recordings from 48 participants yielded 43,923 thirty-second windows. Raw iris distances correlated with EEG alpha (r=+0.118) and theta (r=+0.076), but face scale explained 93% of their variance. After face-width normalisation, alpha remained associated (r=+0.076), whereas theta was not statistically significant. Further adjustment for ocular luminance and head pose rendered alpha nonsignificant (r=+0.021, p=0.33). Circular-shift testing identified alpha coupling in 11/48 participants under full control, versus 28/48 using uncorrected Pearson tests. Within-subject Ridge regression, with no raw sample shared between the training and test windows, yielded a nonsignificant group mean correlation (r=+0.078, p=0.07); 13/48 participants had individually significant prediction-reference associations (11 positive), fewer when the PPG term was restricted to filter-consistent beats. papers.title: Interventional Effects and Neurometabolic Regulation of a Panax quinquefolius-Containing Herbal Extract (JYF) in Diazepam Withdrawal Syndrome in Mice.
papers.abstract: Background: Long-term benzodiazepine use can lead to dependence and clinically significant withdrawal following discontinuation, highlighting the need to identify effective interventions for withdrawal-associated abnormalities. Methods: High-resolution mass spectrometry was used to characterize the constituents of a Panax quinquefolius-containing herbal extract (JYF) and evaluate their in vivo exposure in rats. Sixty-five C57BL/6 mice were randomly assigned to control, model, and low-, medium-, and high-dose JYF groups. Diazepam withdrawal was induced after 28 days of subcutaneous diazepam administration (12 mg/kg), and JYF was administered orally during the peri-withdrawal period for 7 days, beginning 4 days before diazepam discontinuation. Behavioral assessments, electroencephalographic/electromyographic (EEG/EMG) recordings, histopathological analysis, and neurochemical measurements were performed. Network proximity analysis, widely targeted metabolomics, targeted neurotransmitter quantification, and integrated pathway analysis were subsequently performed. Results: A total of 61 constituents were identified in JYF, of which 44 were detected in serum and 34 in brain tissue. Network proximity analysis highlighted genistein, columbamine, jatrorrhizine, and berberine as candidate constituents associated with withdrawal, anxiety/depression and sleep-related modules. JYF attenuated diazepam withdrawal-associated weight loss, anxiety-like behavior, sleep fragmentation, abnormal EEG activity, and elevations in corticosterone and orexin A. Metabolomic analyses revealed disturbances in lipid, energy, and amino acid metabolism, with tryptophan and phenylalanine metabolism emerging as prominent pathways associated with JYF intervention. Diazepam withdrawal also disrupted cerebral monoamine homeostasis, as reflected by increased serotonin and norepinephrine and decreased dopamine levels; these alterations generally shifted toward control levels after JYF intervention. Conclusions: JYF alleviates behavioral and sleep-related abnormalities associated with diazepam withdrawal. Its effects may be associated with alterations in brain metabolic homeostasis, including tryptophan- and phenylalanine-related metabolism and monoaminergic neurotransmission. Genistein and berberine were identified as candidate active constituents that warrant further experimental validation.

papers.title: Association of Total Atherosclerosis Burden of Baroreceptor-Resident Arteries with Heart Rate Variability and Its Circadian Rhythm in Patients with Ischemic Stroke.

However, its association with vascular disease remains incompletely understood. We evaluated associations of atherosclerotic burden in baroreceptor-resident arteries (BRAs), including the carotid sinus (CS) and aortic arch (AA), with heart rate variability (HRV) and its circadian rhythm after ischemic stroke. Methods: This cross-sectional study consecutively enrolled 253 patients with first-ever ischemic stroke within 30 days of onset. Total atherosclerosis burden of baroreceptor-resident arteries (TAB-BRA) was assessed using computed tomography angiography (CTA), and patients were categorized based on TAB-BRA tertiles. The 24 h HRV indices and serial measures across 48 consecutive 30 min segments were derived from Holter recordings, with the standard deviation of all normal-to-normal intervals (SDNN) as the primary outcome. Results: After adjusting for age, sex, hypertension, stroke severity, time from stroke onset to Holter monitoring, and other prespecified covariates, each 1-point increase in TAB-BRA was associated with a 1.67 ms decrease in 24 h SDNN (95% confidence interval [CI], -2.43 to -0.90; p < 0.001), suggesting impaired cardiac autonomic regulation. Restricted cubic spline models revealed a nonlinear association (p for nonlinearity = 0.014). Adding AA burden to the model containing CS burden improved model fit for 24 h SDNN (adjusted R2 difference = 0.033; p = 0.001). Compared with Tertile 1, circadian SDNN amplitude was lower by 3.61 ms in Tertile 2 (95% CI, -6.33 to -0.81; p = 0.006) and 3.71 ms in Tertile 3 (95% CI, -6.59 to -0.77; p = 0.012). Conclusions: Higher TAB-BRA was nonlinearly associated with lower 24 h SDNN, while the intermediate- and high-burden groups had lower circadian SDNN amplitudes. papers.title: Wearable-derived sleep and circadian features associated with electronic health record-documented persistent postsurgical pain.
papers.abstract: A substantial percentage of surgical patients develop persistent postsurgical pain, and sleep disruption is an established, modifiable contributor. Patients later documented with persistent pain showed systematic shifts in wake timing and in heart rate circadian rhythms (elevated amplitude and mesor), with wake timing decoupled from heart rate circadian timing. These changes were absent in a comparison cohort without persistent pain documentation, indicating specificity to persistent postsurgical pain rather than a postoperative or clinical-encounter effect. Findings align with evidence linking altered sleep to pain outcomes and identify cardiac circadian disruption as a distinct marker, suggesting wearable-derived features could capture physiological changes before documentation and inform intervention.

papers.title: Effects of Maternal Caffeine Exposure During Gestation on Neurobehavior, Glucose Metabolism and Circadian Rhythm in Offspring Rats.
papers.abstract: Caffeine intake can have numerous effects on neurological and cognitive impairments. However, its influences on offspring still need to be evaluated. This study aimed to investigate the effects of caffeine exposure during gestation on behavioral development, metabolic function, and circadian rhythms in offspring. A total of 96 Sprague-Dawley rats were included, with an equal number of males and females. After confirming pregnancy, the female rats were randomly divided into four groups on average and administered caffeine at three distinct doses (5, 20, and 80 mg/kg/day) or equivalent volumes of normal saline throughout the gestational period. The health status and weight gain of pregnant rats, as well as the litter size and body weight of offspring, were continuously monitored. Open field test, Morris water maze, intraperitoneal glucose tolerance tests (IPGTT) and intraperitoneal insulin tolerance tests (IPITTs) were performed. The expression levels of 7 circadian clock genes (Bmal1, Clock, Cry1, Cry2, Per1, Per2, and Rev-erbα) were quantified. This revealed a significant reduction in maternal weight gain in the 80 mg/kg caffeine group compared to controls. Although the birth weight of offspring was not significantly affected, the postnatal weight gain of offspring was slower in caffeine groups. Behavioral assessments demonstrated elevated spontaneous activity and increased anxiety-like behaviors in caffeine-exposed offspring. Metabolic evaluations indicated impaired glucose tolerance specifically in female offspring, though no significant alterations were observed in insulin sensitivity, spatial learning and memory performance. Maternal caffeine exposure during gestation also disrupted the rhythmicity of hepatic circadian clock gene expression in offspring rats. These findings suggest that gestational caffeine exposure exerts selective adverse effects on offspring development, behavior, glucose metabolism and circadian rhythm. Caffeine consumption during pregnancy necessitates careful consideration.

Female MSD offspring exhibit delayed-onset glucose intolerance, insulin resistance, and altered lipid utilization during aging, whereas male offspring display only mild metabolic alterations. MSD offspring also demonstrate alterations in anxiety-like and helplessness-related behavioral indices, which are further exacerbated by chronic stress exposure. Transcriptomic analyses reveal coordinated remodeling of hypothalamic neurodevelopmental and neurotransmitter pathways alongside hepatic metabolic programs during fetal development, suggesting early alterations of hypothalamic-liver coupling. Comparative analyses between fetal and adult liver samples demonstrate persistent dysregulation of metabolic pathways. Collectively, these findings suggest that MSD is associated with reconfiguration of fetal central-peripheral regulatory networks, which may contribute to a maladaptive neuro-metabolic trajectory linking metabolic and emotional dysfunction across the lifespan. These results identify prenatal sleep as a modifiable determinant of offspring health and provide insight into potential mechanisms underlying the shared developmental origins of metabolic and affective disorders.

papers.title: Ozone as a Catalyst for Alzheimer's Disease and Sleep Disorders: Implications for Neurodegeneration Induced by Air Pollution.
papers.abstract: Tropospheric ozone, a highly reactive air pollutant, has emerged as a potential environmental risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD) and its associated sleep disturbances, yet a comprehensive synthesis of the underlying mechanisms has remained limited. This narrative review summarizes experimental and epidemiological evidence on ozone exposure, neurodegeneration and disrupted sleep, organized around one working hypothesis: ozone generates a systemic oxidative-inflammatory signal that reaches the central nervous system, with sleep/circadian disruption and AD-related pathology as downstream outcomes that may reinforce each other. In experimental models, ozone is associated with oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, blood-brain barrier disruption, glial activation and neuroinflammation, overlapping with β-amyloid accumulation and tau hyperphosphorylation, and with reduced REM sleep and altered neurotransmitters; clock-gene changes have been shown mainly in peripheral tissue. Circadian disruption is a candidate effector, and current data cannot distinguish mediation from co-occurrence. Epidemiological evidence for ozone-specific associations with cognitive decline remains inconsistent at the population level compared with other pollutants such as PM2.5 or NO2, although some cohorts report pollutant-specific effects and modulation by the apolipoprotein E ε4 (APOE4) genotype. Most experimental studies use concentrations well above regulatory ambient standards. Overall, ambient ozone is a biologically plausible, but not yet epidemiologically confirmed, candidate risk factor for AD and sleep disorders. Future work should prioritize exposure-graded longitudinal studies and clarification of the dose-response relationship, including the effects of controlled medical ozone.

papers.title: Oxidative Stress in Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome: A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Pediatric obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (OSAS) is a common sleep-related breathing disorder increasingly recognized as a multisystem disease rather than an isolated disorder of the upper airway. Recurrent episodes of upper airway obstruction generate intermittent hypoxia, reoxygenation, and sleep fragmentation, promoting excessive production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species and disruption of antioxidant defenses. This narrative review summarizes current evidence regarding the mechanisms, biomarkers, and clinical consequences of oxidative stress in pediatric OSAS. Intermittent hypoxia activates several redox-sensitive pathways, including NADPH oxidases, hypoxia-inducible factor-1α, nuclear factor-κB, mitochondrial dysfunction, and endoplasmic reticulum stress, thereby creating a bidirectional relationship between oxidative stress and systemic inflammation. Pediatric studies have demonstrated alterations in lipid peroxidation products, glutathione redox balance, urinary 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine, isoprostanes, NOX2-related markers, and inflammatory mediators. These abnormalities are associated with endothelial dysfunction and cardiovascular, neurocognitive, metabolic, hepatic, renal, and immune consequences, and several may improve following effective treatment. Importantly, the magnitude of oxidative and end-organ injury does not consistently parallel the apnea-hypopnea index, suggesting that hypoxic burden, obesity, genetic susceptibility, antioxidant capacity, and disease duration influence individual biological vulnerability. Although several oxidative biomarkers show potential for disease characterization and treatment monitoring, methodological heterogeneity and the absence of standardized pediatric reference values currently limit their clinical application. Future integration of polysomnographic hypoxic-burden metrics with oxidative, inflammatory, metabolomic, and genomic biomarkers may improve risk stratification and facilitate more personalized management of pediatric OSAS.

papers.title: Multi-omics analysis reveals that sleep deprivation exacerbates intestinal barrier injury via the microbiota-dependent taurodeoxycholic acid/group 3 innate lymphoid/IL-22 axis.

The dynamic changes in the intestinal microenvironment were systematically profiled using multi-omics approaches, including metagenomic sequencing, untargeted metabolomics and RNA sequencing. The causal role of microbial dysbiosis and the underlying mechanisms were further investigated using germ-free mice, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), flow cytometry, and targeted intervention. Distinct microbial communities and metabolite profiles were observed among brief SD (< 24 h of SD), prolonged SD (24-96 h of SD) and control. Supplementation with TDCA effectively restored ILC3 function, IL-22 production, and barrier integrity in SD mice. Furthermore, FMT from patients with sleep dysfunction significantly disturbed intestinal microenvironment and increased serum cortisol by regulating gut microbiota and inhibiting TDCA/ILC3/IL-22 axis. This study dynamically delineates how SD disrupts intestinal homeostasis by reshaping the gut microbiota and suppressing the TDCA/ILC3/IL-22 axis. Menopausal symptoms were evaluated using the Simplified Menopausal Index, including vasomotor, psychological, and somatic domains, with higher scores indicating greater symptom burden. The consistency of the findings across sensitivity analyses supports the robustness of this association. Sleep complaints may therefore serve as an accessible signal for recognizing menopausal symptom burden in clinical and occupational health settings.

papers.title: Effects of 24-h sleep deprivation on circulating irisin, BDNF, and soluble klotho responses during exercise in the heat in young and older males.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation and heat stress commonly coexist in occupational, athletic, and environmental settings and may disproportionately increase physiological strain in older adults. We examined whether 24-h sleep deprivation alters circulating biomarkers linked to proposed roles in metabolic adaptation (irisin), neurophysiological regulation (BDNF), and cellular stress protection (soluble klotho) during exercise in the heat in young and older males. Ten young (23±3 years) and ten older (61±4 years) males completed randomized crossover trials involving normal sleep and 24-h total sleep deprivation before three 30-min bouts of semi-recumbent cycling in hot, dry conditions (40°C, ∼13% relative humidity). Blood samples were obtained before and at end-exercise for measurement of irisin, BDNF, and soluble klotho (s-klotho). Older males exhibited lower circulating concentrations of all three biomarkers across conditions and time points than young males. Exercise in the heat increased irisin (mean change 522.7 pg/mL, 95% CI 310.6 to 734.8, p<0.001, q<0.001), whereas no statistically significant overall pre-to-end change was observed for BDNF or s-klotho. The irisin response appeared smaller in older than young males when averaged across sleep conditions (between-group difference 458.1 pg/mL, 95% CI 34.0 to 882.3, p=0.035) but did not remain significant after correction across the three age × time contrasts (q=0.104) and is therefore hypothesis-generating. However, the study did not detect evidence that 24-h sleep deprivation altered circulating irisin, BDNF, or s-klotho responses in either age group. These findings demonstrate age-related differences in circulating biomarker concentrations, but do not establish corresponding differences in physiological adaptability or biomarker responsiveness.

papers.title: Sleep Disturbances and Circadian Phase Delay in People Living with Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV): A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Advances in HIV research and antiretroviral therapy (ART) have substantially increased life expectancy among people living with HIV (PLHIV). However, challenges affecting quality of life and alterations in daily physiological processes persist. Among the health dimensions most affected are sleep quality and circadian rhythms, resulting in significant biological alterations. The main objective of this study is to analyze the existing scientific evidence regarding the effects of HIV on sleep quality and on the alignment and synchronization of circadian rhythms. The bidirectional interaction between these physiological alterations and associated clinical, immunological, and metabolic factors in people living with HIV (PLHIV) was evaluated, emphasizing their integration. For this review, searches were conducted in the PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases. Eligibility criteria were applied, resulting in a final selection of 15 studies based on search strategies. The findings demonstrated a high prevalence of poor sleep quality as well as delayed circadian phase. These chronobiological alterations were closely associated with systemic inflammation, altered melatonin levels, impaired cognitive performance, and an altered metabolic profile involving leptin, ghrelin, adiponectin, and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) signaling. Despite the consistency of the results, the methodologies of individual studies varied, and a notable absence of clinical trials aimed at addressing poor sleep quality and chronodisruption was observed. A promising clinical approach involves complementing antiretroviral therapy (ART) with chronotherapeutic interventions and sleep hygiene. In conclusion, HIV can disrupt personal temporal organization at a systemic level; consequently, incorporating assessments of sleep and circadian rhythms into clinical care may be warranted, while chronotherapeutic interventions should be further investigated.

papers.title: Exploratory Metabolomic and Metagenomic Profiling of Fecal Samples in Isolated REM Sleep Behavior Disorder.
papers.abstract: Isolated REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD) is among the most reliable prodromal markers of α-synucleinopathies. Under the body-first (gut-first) model of α-synuclein pathology, in which pathology may originate in the enteric nervous system and ascend to the brain, the gut is a biologically plausible compartment in which early and accessible molecular alterations might be detectable; however, the fecal metabolome remains poorly investigated in this population. In this exploratory, cross-sectional study of 21 iRBD patients and 15 healthy controls, we characterized fecal samples through an integrated multi-omics framework. The fecal metabolome was profiled on two complementary mass spectrometry platforms: HS-SPME GC-EI-high-resolution MS, used for both untargeted volatilomics and targeted quantification of linear and branched short-chain fatty acids, and untargeted LC-MS/MS for the non-volatile fraction. Gut microbial community composition was characterized on the same material by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and the metabolomic and microbial layers were combined by DIABLO multi-omics integration. Linear short-chain fatty acids were preserved, whereas branched-chain fatty acids were selectively increased in iRBD, indicating a shift toward proteolytic fermentation. Volatile indole was reduced, while p-cresol and 2-octanone were increased, paralleled at the LC-MS/MS level by attenuation of the tryptophan-indole axis, class-level bile acid depletion, and increased acylcarnitines. The microbiome was depleted of Blautia and Faecalibacterium and enriched in Oscillospirales. Integration resolved a coherent host-microbe signature that discriminated iRBD patients from controls within this discovery cohort (84.8% cross-validated accuracy). These cross-sectional findings characterize candidate fecal signatures associated with iRBD; given the exploratory design and the limited sample size, they are hypothesis-generating, and their value for predicting phenoconversion remains to be established in prospective studies.

papers.title: Early Post-Operative Quantitative EEG Central Beta Power Predicts Futile Recanalization After Endovascular Treatment in AIS-LVO.
papers.abstract: Despite successful endovascular recanalization in acute ischemic stroke, approximately 50%-55% of patients experience 90-day futile recanalization (FR). We evaluated the prognostic value of central relative beta power derived from early postoperative quantitative electroencephalography (QEEG) and explored QEEG associations with brain edema and parenchymal hemorrhage. This retrospective, single-center subgroup analysis of the prospective multicenter DETECT2-China registry included 56 patients with acute ischemic stroke due to large-vessel occlusion. Patients underwent 20-30-min EEG recordings approximately 24 h after successful endovascular treatment. Multivariable logistic regression adjusting for seven clinical covariates, Firth and reduced-model sensitivity analyses, and leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) with the DeLong test were performed. An additional sensitivity analysis repeated QEEG feature selection within each training set. Feature reliability was evaluated using split-half intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). Of 56 patients, 31 (55.4%) developed 90-day FR. Higher central relative beta power was independently associated with lower odds of FR (adjusted OR: 0.28 per 1-SD increase, 95% CI: 0.11-0.74, p = 0.010). Integrating central beta power into the clinical model increased the fixed-feature LOOCV area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) from 0.557 to 0.719 (DeLong p = 0.007). In exploratory analyses, delta-band Brain Symmetry Index specifically tracked parenchymal hemorrhage (PH vs. no intracranial hemorrhage [No ICH], p = 0.006). Exploratory graph analysis also showed macro-scale network disintegration in FR patients. All QEEG features demonstrated high split-half reliability (ICC ≥ 0.75). Central relative beta power recorded approximately 24 h after endovascular treatment was independently associated with 90-day FR and showed potential incremental prognostic value. Exploratory associations with postoperative complications suggest that QEEG may provide a non-invasive bedside "brain window" for neurocritical care.

papers.title: Effects of Sleep Deprivation on Oral Health: A Literature Review.
papers.abstract: Oral health and sleep health are rarely discussed in the same clinical conversation, yet the biological evidence linking them is both substantial and growing. Chronic sleep deprivation triggers a cascade of systemic disruptions, including immune dysregulation, hormonal imbalance, and oxidative stress, which leave unmistakable marks on the oral cavity. Despite this, sleep analysis remains largely absent from routine dental assessment, and its role as an independent driver of oral disease has yet to receive the clinical attention it deserves. This article provides a comprehensive narrative review of the mechanisms through which sleep deprivation compromises oral health, organized around five interconnected domains: the immunological consequences of sleep loss, including its role in periodontal destruction and impaired mucosal healing; disruptions to the salivary environment and their downstream effects on caries, xerostomia, and halitosis; behavioral and lifestyle mediators such as glycemic dysregulation, tobacco use, and caffeine consumption; neuromuscular and structural consequences encompassing bruxism, temporomandibular dysfunction, traumatic dental injuries, and dysphagia; and obstructive sleep apnea as a major oral health comorbidity that both reflects and reinforces sleep deficiency. The article further addresses the practical implications of these findings for clinical dental practice, outlining how dentists can incorporate sleep-related screening into routine assessments through validated questionnaires, anatomical risk evaluation, and recognition of characteristic oral markers, and when referral to a sleep medicine specialist is warranted. The evidence reviewed here positions sleep deprivation as a significant, independent risk factor for a broad range of oral conditions and supports the integration of sleep health into a more comprehensive, patient-centered model of dental care.

It argues that sleep deprivation is an independent risk factor for oral conditions and outlines dental screening and referral practices.

papers.title: Seasonal Variation, Circadian Patterns, and Night Eating Syndrome Among Older Adults: The Mediating Role of Sleep Quality.
papers.abstract: Objective: We aimed to examine whether sleep quality mediates the relationship between seasonal variation, circadian pattern, and night eating syndrome in community-dwelling older adults. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted with 336 community-dwelling older adults (aged ≥ 60 years) recruited from geriatric social clubs. Participants completed validated instruments, including the Global Seasonality Scale (GSS), Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ), Night Eating Diagnostic Questionnaire (NEDQ), and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Path analysis with bootstrapping (5000 resamples) was used to estimate direct and indirect associations among the study variables. Results: The mean age was 66.8 ± 5.9 years (56.8% male). Moderate to severe seasonal variation was observed in 68.2% of participants, while 85.1% reported poor sleep quality. Morning circadian pattern predominated (56.9%), and 23.2% met criteria for full night eating syndrome. Path analysis identified a significant indirect association between seasonal variation and circadian pattern through sleep quality (B = -0.038, 95% CI [-0.051, -0.026]), corresponding to 41% of the total modeled association. Similarly, a significant indirect association between seasonal variation and night eating syndrome through sleep quality was observed (B = 0.053, 95% CI [0.037, 0.068]), corresponding to 37% of the total modeled association. All direct and indirect paths were statistically significant (p < 0.001). Conclusions: Sleep quality was significantly involved in the observed relationships between seasonal variation, circadian pattern, and night eating syndrome among older adults, with the path models indicating both direct and indirect associations. These findings emphasize the interconnected nature of seasonal sensitivity, sleep characteristics, circadian preference, and nighttime eating behavior in later life. Further longitudinal research with repeated seasonal assessments is warranted to clarify the temporal relationships among these factors and to determine the potential value of sleep-focused preventive and clinical approaches.

papers.title: Depressive Symptoms, Insomnia-Related Difficulties and Self-Rated Health Among Community-Dwelling Adults Aged 40 Years and Older in Western China: A Cross-Sectional Structural Equation Modelling Study.
papers.abstract: This study examined the associations of depressive symptoms, medical help-seeking attitudes and perceived neighbourhood built environment with self-rated health, including statistical indirect associations through an Insomnia Severity Index (ISI)-derived sleep construct, among community-dwelling adults in western China. This secondary cross-sectional analysis included 433 adults aged ≥40 years in Gaoping District, Nanchong, China. Self-rated health was assessed using the SF-36 General Health subscale. PHQ-9 and ISI indicators were reverse-coded so that higher values represented lower depressive symptom burden and fewer insomnia-related difficulties, respectively. Structural equation modelling estimated direct and indirect associations, with 5000 bootstrap resamples. Multi-group analysis compared the ISI-self-rated health path between family-functioning groups. Model fit indices were CFI = 0.955, TLI = 0.953 and RMSEA = 0.037. The ISI-derived construct had the largest standardised direct coefficient for self-rated health (β = 0.383, p < 0.001). Reverse-coded PHQ-9 was associated with ISI (β = 0.544, p < 0.001) and self-rated health (β = 0.164, p = 0.009). Medical help-seeking attitudes were directly associated with self-rated health (β = 0.193, p = 0.001). The PHQ-9-ISI-self-rated health indirect estimate was 0.208 (95% CI, 0.134-0.294). Corresponding indirect associations for help-seeking attitudes and neighbourhood environment were not supported. NEWS-A direct paths and the family-functioning group difference were not statistically significant. The findings supported an ISI-related statistical indirect association between depressive symptoms and self-rated health within the specified model. They do not establish causal mediation or intervention effectiveness.

papers.title: Assessment of night eating syndrome and circadian-related characteristics among university students of Rawalpindi and Islamabad.
papers.abstract: Non-communicable diseases are associated with lifestyle behaviors such as diet, meal timing, levels of stress, quality of sleep, and disruption of circadian rhythms. Night Eating Syndrome (NES) is an abnormal eating behavior characterized by eating at night and/or eating after the last meal of the day. NES may be associated with sleep disturbances and/or circadian-related characteristics. University students are particularly susceptible to the development of NES due to academic stress, irregular schedules, increased exposure to screens, and late nights. This study aimed to determine the prevalence and severity of Night Eating Syndrome and to examine the relationships between Night Eating Syndrome and sleep-related characteristics, circadian-related characteristics (diurnal preference), and mood among university students in Rawalpindi and Islamabad, Pakistan. A cross-sectional analytical study was conducted on 335 undergraduate university students at four universities in Rawalpindi and Islamabad using a multistage sampling method. Data were collected using structured questionnaires including sociodemographic questions, the Night Eating Diagnostic Questionnaire, and the Sleep, Circadian Rhythm, and Mood questionnaire. Data analysis was performed using SPSS Version 27. Descriptive statistics, one-way ANOVA, Welch's ANOVA with Games-Howell post-hoc comparisons, multiple linear regression, Fisher-Freeman-Halton exact test, and Pearson chi-square test were used, with significance set at p < 0.05. The Prevalence of Night Eating Syndrome was 6% (n = 18; 95% CI: 3.2-8.4%). Severity-based classification showed that 51.0% had normal scores, 26.3% had mild symptoms, 17.3% had moderate symptoms, and 6% met the NEDQ criteria for NES. There were significant differences between NES severity groups in Morningness and Good Sleep scores (p < 0.001), while there were no significant differences in Depressed Mood scores (p = 0.159). In adjusted regression models, NES status was significantly associated with Good Sleep scores, while sex was associated with Morningness and BMI was associated with Depressed Mood. BMI category was significantly associated with NES status (Fisher-Freeman-Halton exact test, p = 0.002) and NES severity (p < 0.001). Night Eating Syndrome and related symptoms were present among university students, with increasing symptom severity associated with differences in Morningness and Good Sleep scores, while Depressed Mood did not differ significantly across severity categories. These findings suggest the possible significance of health promotion initiatives conducted through universities emphasizing good sleep hygiene, regular meal time and early identification of night eating symptoms.

papers.title: Migraine burden and occupational impact among corporate employees attending neurology clinics in Skardu, Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan.
papers.abstract: Objectives. Migraine is a leading cause of disability worldwide, yet remains underdiagnosed in low and middle-income countries. This study assessed the clinical features, triggers, management patterns and occupational impact of neurologist-diagnosed migraine among corporate employees in Skardu, Pakistan. Methods. A cross-sectional study of adult corporate employees with neurologist-confirmed migraine was conducted at neurology outpatient clinics in Skardu, Gilgit-Baltistan. Data were collected via a validated questionnaire on demographics, clinical features, triggers, occupational impact and management. Non-parametric tests and multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of high occupational impact, reported as adjusted odds ratios and p values. Results. Most participants were female (72.4%) and aged 26-35 years (43.0%), with migraine without aura being the most common (40.6%). The mean migraine burden was high (58.9 ± 13.6) and varied significantly by gender, age and management. Poor management (34.7%) and reliance on Over-the-Counter (OTC) analgesics (65.3%) were common. Work impact was substantial, with 44% reporting moderate-to-severe absenteeism and 55% presenteeism. High occupational impact was independently predicted by higher migraine burden, frequent attacks (>6/month), stress, sleep deprivation, environmental stressors, poor management and information technology-sector employment. Conclusion. Among corporate employees in Skardu, migraine causes significant absenteeism and workplace impairment; addressing triggers and improving specialist care can reduce disability.
